# Education in China: Summary
Education in China has undergone significant transformation since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. Initially focused on improving literacy through formal schooling and literacy campaigns, China has expanded education access dramatically, enforcing a nine-year compulsory education law since 1986 covering six years of primary and three years of junior secondary education. Education reforms have devolved many responsibilities to local governments, with efforts focused on economic modernization, vocational and technical training, and scientific development aligned with the country's Four Modernizations policy. While education quality and access have improved, regional disparities and issues related to teacher shortages and rural schooling persist.
The Chinese education system is structured into elementary (grades 1–6), middle (grades 7–9), and high school (grades 10–12) levels, with a strong emphasis on core academic subjects and political education. Vocational education forms a substantial part of secondary education, though it faces challenges related to perception and resource allocation. Higher education in China is the largest worldwide, comprising over 3,000 institutions with growing international recognition, propelled by initiatives like the Double First-Class Construction plan to develop world-class universities. Admission remains highly competitive, governed mainly by national examinations (Gaokao), with a growing trend of Chinese students pursuing studies abroad. Recent government policies emphasize ideological education, limit homework and private tutoring, and exert stringent control over curricula and teaching materials to align education with socialist values. Despite remarkable academic achievements at international assessments, challenges remain regarding rigor, memorization emphasis, regional inequality, and academic freedom.
